```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(lantern)
```

## Overview

lantern splits each sample's alternate-allele dosage at a variant into
one dosage per ancestral population. There are two ways to do this:

| Mode | Uses | How an allele is assigned |
|------|------|---------------------------|
| Phased (`"haplotype"`) | the allele and the ancestry of each haplotype | to the population of the haplotype that carries it |
| Unphased (`"dosage"`) | the genotype (0/1/2) and the pair of ancestries at the site | shared by estimated proportions when the genotype is ambiguous |

This vignette explains both on small matrices, without any files, using
the low-level functions that `ancestry_split()` calls internally. Part A
covers two populations, Part B any number of populations, and Part C the
shrinkage that `ancestry_split()` applies to unphased splits.
`vignette("toy-vcf-msp-example")` shows the same splits starting from VCF
and MSP files.

***

# Part A: Two populations

## A.1 Unphased split with `split_diploid()`

Without phase we only know, for each sample at a variant, its genotype (0,
1 or 2 alternate alleles) and its pair of ancestries, coded as

* 1 = EUR/EUR (both haplotypes European),
* 2 = AFR/EUR (one of each),
* 3 = AFR/AFR.

For most samples the split is obvious. An AFR/AFR sample's alleles are all
African, and an AFR/EUR sample with genotype 2 has one allele on each
haplotype, so one African and one European. The only ambiguous case is an
AFR/EUR heterozygote: it has one alternate allele, and we cannot tell
which haplotype carries it.

Consider a single variant in six samples:

```{r a1-data}
gt  <- matrix(c(1, 2, 1, 1, 0, 2), nrow = 1,
              dimnames = list("var1", paste0("S", 1:6)))
anc <- matrix(c(3, 3, 1, 2, 2, 2), nrow = 1,
              dimnames = list("var1", paste0("S", 1:6)))
rbind(genotype = gt[1, ], ancestry = anc[1, ])
```

S1 and S2 are AFR/AFR carriers, S3 is a EUR/EUR carrier, S6 is an AFR/EUR
homozygote and S4 is the one ambiguous AFR/EUR heterozygote. To split S4's
allele we estimate how this variant's alternate alleles divide between
African and European haplotypes, using only the unambiguous carriers.
Writing \(N\) for the number of samples of a given ancestry and genotype,

\[
p_\text{AFR} = \frac{2N_\text{AFR/AFR, 2} + N_\text{AFR/AFR, 1} + N_\text{AFR/EUR, 2}}{D},
\qquad
p_\text{EUR} = \frac{N_\text{AFR/EUR, 2} + 2N_\text{EUR/EUR, 2} + N_\text{EUR/EUR, 1}}{D},
\]

where \(D\) is the number of unambiguous alternate alleles, that is, all
alternate alleles at the variant minus those of the ambiguous
heterozygotes:

\[
D = 2N_\text{AFR/AFR, 2} + N_\text{AFR/AFR, 1} + 2N_\text{AFR/EUR, 2}
  + 2N_\text{EUR/EUR, 2} + N_\text{EUR/EUR, 1}.
\]

An AFR/EUR homozygote contributes one allele to each population. The
ambiguous heterozygote then gets \(p_\text{AFR}\) of its allele as African
dosage and \(p_\text{EUR}\) as European dosage. For our variant:

```{r a1-by-hand}
n <- function(a, g) sum(anc == a & gt == g)
D <- 2 * n(3, 2) + n(3, 1) + 2 * n(2, 2) + 2 * n(1, 2) + n(1, 1)
p_afr <- (2 * n(3, 2) + n(3, 1) + n(2, 2)) / D
p_eur <- (n(2, 2) + 2 * n(1, 2) + n(1, 1)) / D
c(D = D, p_AFR = p_afr, p_EUR = p_eur)
```

`split_diploid()` returns the two dosage matrices. S4's allele is split
2/3 African and 1/3 European, and every other sample's split is whole:

```{r a1-split}
res <- split_diploid(gt, anc)
split_table <- rbind(AFR = res$african[1, ], EUR = res$european[1, ])
colnames(split_table) <- colnames(gt)
split_table
```

If every carrier of a variant is an ambiguous heterozygote, \(D = 0\) and
the proportions cannot be estimated. `split_diploid()` then splits each
allele 1/2 and 1/2:

```{r a1-edge}
gt_edge  <- matrix(c(1, 0, 1), nrow = 1)
anc_edge <- matrix(c(2, 1, 2), nrow = 1)
split_diploid(gt_edge, anc_edge)
```

Part C shows that estimates from very few unambiguous carriers are also
unreliable, and how `ancestry_split()` handles that.

## A.2 Phased split with `split_haplotype()`

With phased genotypes and local ancestry for each haplotype, nothing needs
to be estimated: each haplotype's allele goes to that haplotype's
population. `split_haplotype()` takes four matrices of the same shape
(variants x samples): the alleles (0/1) on haplotype 0 and on haplotype 1,
and the ancestry of each haplotype, with RFMix's codes 0 = AFR and
1 = EUR.

```{r a2-data}
ids <- list(paste0("var", 1:3), paste0("S", 1:3))
gt0 <- matrix(c(1, 0, 1,  0, 1, 0,  1, 1, 0), nrow = 3, dimnames = ids)
gt1 <- matrix(c(0, 1, 0,  1, 0, 1,  0, 1, 1), nrow = 3, dimnames = ids)
a0  <- matrix(c(0, 0, 1,  1, 0, 0,  0, 1, 0), nrow = 3, dimnames = ids)
a1  <- matrix(c(1, 1, 0,  0, 1, 1,  1, 0, 1), nrow = 3, dimnames = ids)
```

Take S1 at `var1`: haplotype 0 carries the allele (`gt0` is 1) and is
African (`a0` is 0), and haplotype 1 does not carry it. So S1 has an
African dosage of 1 and a European dosage of 0 at `var1`.

```{r a2-split}
phased <- split_haplotype(gt0, gt1, a0, a1)
phased$african
phased$european
```

The two dosages always add up to the genotype, `gt0 + gt1`:

```{r a2-total}
all.equal(phased$african + phased$european, unname(gt0 + gt1))
```

***

# Part B: More than two populations

`split_diploid_multi()` and `split_haplotype_multi()` do the same for any
number of populations K. With two populations they give the same results
as the functions in Part A.

## B.1 Unphased split with `split_diploid_multi()`

With K populations a sample's pair of ancestries is either pure (both
haplotypes from the same population) or mixed (from two different
populations). There are K pure and K(K-1)/2 mixed combinations:

| K | Pure | Mixed | Total codes |
|---|------|-------|-------------|
| 2 | 2 | 1 | 3 |
| 3 | 3 | 3 | 6 |
| 4 | 4 | 6 | 10 |

You choose a code for each combination and pass two descriptions to the
function: `pure_codes`, the code of each pure combination, and
`mixed_codes`, a table with the code and the two populations of each
mixed combination. For three populations (African, European and Native
American):

```{r b1-codes}
pure_codes  <- c(AFR = 3L, EUR = 1L, NAT = 4L)
mixed_codes <- data.frame(code = c(2L, 5L, 6L),
                          pop1 = c("AFR", "AFR", "EUR"),
                          pop2 = c("EUR", "NAT", "NAT"))
mixed_codes
```

We simulate 12 rare variants in 30 samples from a three-way admixed
group:

```{r b1-data}
set.seed(2025)
gt3 <- matrix(sample(0:2, 12 * 30, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.88, 0.10, 0.02)),
              nrow = 12, ncol = 30)
anc3 <- matrix(sample(c(pure_codes, mixed_codes$code), 12 * 30, replace = TRUE,
                      prob = c(0.30, 0.20, 0.10, 0.20, 0.10, 0.10)),
               nrow = 12, ncol = 30)
out <- split_diploid_multi(gt3, anc3, pure_codes, mixed_codes)
names(out)
```

The estimate works as in A.1, with one proportion per population. Pure
carriers count for their population and mixed homozygotes contribute one
allele to each of their two populations. With \(N_{k,g}\) the number of
pure population-\(k\) samples with genotype \(g\), and \(N_{\{k,j\},2}\)
the number of mixed \(k\)/\(j\) homozygotes,

\[
p_k = \frac{2N_{k,2} + N_{k,1} + \sum_{j \ne k} N_{\{k,j\},2}}{D},
\qquad
D = \sum_k \left(2N_{k,2} + N_{k,1}\right) + 2\sum_{k<j} N_{\{k,j\},2},
\]

so the \(p_k\) add up to 1. An ambiguous heterozygote with ancestries
\(i\) and \(j\) then gets \(p_i / (p_i + p_j)\) of its allele in
population \(i\) and \(p_j / (p_i + p_j)\) in population \(j\).

To check this, we take the first variant with an ambiguous AFR/EUR
heterozygote and compute the proportions by hand:

```{r b1-by-hand}
v <- which(rowSums(anc3 == 2 & gt3 == 1) > 0)[1]
g <- gt3[v, ]
a <- anc3[v, ]
n <- function(code, genotype) sum(a == code & g == genotype)
num <- c(AFR = 2 * n(3, 2) + n(3, 1) + n(2, 2) + n(5, 2),
         EUR = 2 * n(1, 2) + n(1, 1) + n(2, 2) + n(6, 2),
         NAT = 2 * n(4, 2) + n(4, 1) + n(5, 2) + n(6, 2))
p <- num / sum(num)   # sum(num) equals D
p
```

The heterozygote's African share should be \(p_\text{AFR} / (p_\text{AFR}
+ p_\text{EUR})\), which matches the function's output:

```{r b1-check}
s <- which(a == 2 & g == 1)[1]
c(by_hand  = unname(p["AFR"] / (p["AFR"] + p["EUR"])),
  lantern  = out$AFR[v, s])
```

## B.2 Phased split with `split_haplotype_multi()`

The phased split needs only the code of each population, as used in the
MSP file (RFMix numbers populations from 0):

```{r b2-split}
set.seed(2025)
hap0 <- matrix(rbinom(8 * 6, 1, 0.1), nrow = 8)
hap1 <- matrix(rbinom(8 * 6, 1, 0.1), nrow = 8)
anc0 <- matrix(sample(0:2, 8 * 6, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.4, 0.4, 0.2)), nrow = 8)
anc1 <- matrix(sample(0:2, 8 * 6, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.4, 0.4, 0.2)), nrow = 8)

phased3 <- split_haplotype_multi(hap0, hap1, anc0, anc1,
                                 pop_codes = c(AFR = 0L, EUR = 1L, NAT = 2L))
phased3$AFR[1:4, ]
```

Each allele goes to exactly one population, so the three dosages add up
to the genotype:

```{r b2-total}
all.equal(phased3$AFR + phased3$EUR + phased3$NAT, hap0 + hap1)
```

With two populations, `split_haplotype_multi()` gives the same result as
`split_haplotype()`:

```{r b2-equivalent}
m2 <- split_haplotype_multi(gt0, gt1, a0, a1, pop_codes = c(AFR = 0L, EUR = 1L))
all.equal(unname(m2$AFR), phased$african)
```

## B.3 Four or more populations

More populations only means more entries in `pure_codes` and more rows in
`mixed_codes`, one for every pair of populations. For four populations:

```{r b3-four}
pure_4  <- c(AFR = 3L, EUR = 1L, NAT = 4L, EAS = 5L)
mixed_4 <- data.frame(code = c(2L, 6L, 7L, 8L, 9L, 10L),
                      pop1 = c("AFR", "AFR", "AFR", "EUR", "EUR", "NAT"),
                      pop2 = c("EUR", "NAT", "EAS", "NAT", "EAS", "EAS"))

set.seed(11)
gt4  <- matrix(sample(0:2, 6 * 16, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.85, 0.12, 0.03)),
               nrow = 6)
anc4 <- matrix(sample(c(pure_4, mixed_4$code), 6 * 16, replace = TRUE), nrow = 6)
out4 <- split_diploid_multi(gt4, anc4, pure_4, mixed_4)
names(out4)
```

***

# Part C: Shrinkage toward 1/2

The proportions in A.1 and B.1 are estimated from the unambiguous carriers
of each variant. Rare variants have few carriers, and an estimate from one
or two of them can be far from the truth. Consider a variant carried by ten
ambiguous AFR/EUR heterozygotes and a single EUR/EUR homozygote:

```{r c-data}
gt_dom  <- matrix(c(rep(1L, 10), 2L), nrow = 1)
anc_dom <- matrix(c(rep(2L, 10), 1L), nrow = 1)
raw <- split_diploid_multi(gt_dom, anc_dom, pure_codes, mixed_codes)
c(AFR = sum(raw$AFR), EUR = sum(raw$EUR), NAT = sum(raw$NAT))
```

The only unambiguous carrier is European, so the estimate is
\(p_\text{EUR} = 1\), and all ten ambiguous alleles are assigned to
European haplotypes on the strength of one sample.

`ancestry_split()` therefore pulls the estimated share toward 1/2. How
far depends on \(w\), the fraction of the variant's alternate alleles
that are ambiguous (homozygotes count twice, as they carry two alleles).
For an ambiguous heterozygote with ancestries \(i\) and \(j\),

\[
\text{share}_i = (1 - w)\,\frac{p_i}{p_i + p_j} + w \cdot \frac{1}{2}.
\]

When most of the evidence is unambiguous, \(w\) is close to 0 and the
estimate from A.1 or B.1 is used almost unchanged. When there is no
unambiguous evidence, \(w = 1\) and the allele is split exactly 1/2 and
1/2, the same as the fallback in A.1. The shares stay within the pair, so
an AFR/EUR heterozygote never gets Native American dosage.

The target is 1/2 because an AFR/EUR heterozygote has exactly one African
and one European haplotype at the site. Which of the two carries the
allele depends on how common the allele is on African versus European
haplotypes, not on how much African ancestry the cohort has overall. An
earlier version of lantern shrank toward the cohort's average ancestry
(about 0.82 African on chromosome 19 in our data). In simulations based on
that data, ambiguous alleles were in fact on the African haplotype half of
the time, and shrinking toward 1/2 assigned them more accurately.

The low-level functions take the target through their `gla` argument (one
row of target proportions) and `arm_id` (which row each variant uses). A
target of 1/K for each of K populations gives 1/2 for every pair, which is
what `ancestry_split()` uses:

```{r c-shrink}
half <- matrix(1/3, nrow = 1, ncol = 3,
               dimnames = list("all", c("AFR", "EUR", "NAT")))
shrunk <- split_diploid_multi(gt_dom, anc_dom, pure_codes, mixed_codes,
                              gla = half, arm_id = 0L)
rbind(raw    = c(AFR = sum(raw$AFR), EUR = sum(raw$EUR)),
      shrunk = c(AFR = sum(shrunk$AFR), EUR = sum(shrunk$EUR)))
```

Here 10 of the variant's 12 alternate alleles are ambiguous, so
\(w = 10/12\). Each heterozygote's African share becomes
\((2/12) \cdot 0 + (10/12) \cdot (1/2) = 5/12 \approx 0.42\) instead of 0:

```{r c-share}
shrunk$AFR[1, 1]
```

The variant from A.1 has much more unambiguous evidence: one ambiguous
allele out of seven, so \(w = 1/7\), and S4's African share moves only
slightly, from 2/3 to \((6/7)(2/3) + (1/7)(1/2) = 9/14 \approx 0.64\):

```{r c-a1}
# S4 is the 4th sample
split_diploid(gt, anc, gla = matrix(0.5, nrow = 1, ncol = 2), arm_id = 0L)$african[1, 4]
```

You do not need to set the target yourself: `ancestry_split(mode =
"dosage")` always applies it.
